claim: Dimorphic amino acids at positions 77 and 80 delineate HLA-C allotypes into two groups, C1 and C2.
source: Dimorphic amino acids at positions 77 and 80 delineate HLA-C allotypes into two groups, C1 and C2, which associate with disease through interactions with C1 and C2-specific natural killer cell receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HLA-C classification and is cited in the introduction with references to the literature.

claim: C1 and C2 HLA-C groups associate with disease through interactions with C1 and C2-specific natural killer cell receptors.
source: Dimorphic amino acids at positions 77 and 80 delineate HLA-C allotypes into two groups, C1 and C2, which associate with disease through interactions with C1 and C2-specific natural killer cell receptors.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction discussing disease associations.

claim: KRAS-G12D neoantigen-specific T cell receptors (TCRs) discriminated between C1 and C2 presenting the same KRAS-G12D peptides.
source: Using HLA-C allotypes that differ only by the C1/C2-defining residues, we found that KRAS-G12D neoantigen-specific T cell receptors (TCRs) discriminated between C1 and C2 presenting the same KRAS-G12D peptides.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 3, and functional assays throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ser77 in C1 and Asn77 in C2 influence amino acid preference near the peptide C-terminus (pΩ), including the pΩ-1 position.
source: Structural and functional experiments, and immunopeptidomics analysis revealed that Ser77 in C1 and Asn77 in C2 influence amino acid preference near the peptide C-terminus (pΩ), including the pΩ-1 position, in which C1 favors small and C2 prefers large residues.
evidence: This is supported by structural data in Figure 5, immunopeptidomics analysis in Figure 6, and functional experiments in Figure 7.

claim: C1 favors small residues at the pΩ-1 position and C2 prefers large residues at the pΩ-1 position.
source: Structural and functional experiments, and immunopeptidomics analysis revealed that Ser77 in C1 and Asn77 in C2 influence amino acid preference near the peptide C-terminus (pΩ), including the pΩ-1 position, in which C1 favors small and C2 prefers large residues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunopeptidomics data in Figure 6 showing enrichment of small residues (Ser, Ala, Pro) in C1 and large residues (Phe, Leu, Lys, Met, Arg, Trp, Tyr) in C2.

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism resulted in weaker TCR affinity for KRAS-G12D-bound C2-HLA-C despite conserved TCR contacts.
source: This resulted in weaker TCR affinity for KRAS-G12D-bound C2-HLA-C despite conserved TCR contacts.
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data in Figure 3 showing reduced affinity of TCR9a and TCR10 for C2 compared to C1, and structural data in Figure 4 showing conserved TCR contacts.

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism impacts peptide presentation and HLA-C-restricted T cell responses.
source: Thus, the C1/C2 dimorphism on its own impacts peptide presentation and HLA-C-restricted T cell responses, with implications in disease, including adoptive T cell therapy targeting KRAS-G12D-induced cancers.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing differential peptide binding (Figure 2), TCR recognition (Figures 1, 3), and structural differences (Figures 4, 5).

claim: HLA-C is thought to play a lesser role in T cell responses compared to HLA-A and HLA-B due to its lower cell surface expression level.
source: HLA-C is thought to play a lesser role in T cell responses compared to that of HLA-A and HLA-B due to its lower cell surface expression level (Apps et al., 2015; McCutcheon et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HLA-C allotypes with high expression were associated with increased T cell responses and slower progression to AIDS in HIV infection.
source: In HIV infection, HLA-C allotypes with a high expression were associated with increased T cell responses and slower progression to AIDS, while higher HLA-C expression was also linked with susceptibility to Crohn's disease (Apps et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Apps et al., 2013.

claim: Higher HLA-C expression was linked with susceptibility to Crohn's disease.
source: In HIV infection, HLA-C allotypes with a high expression were associated with increased T cell responses and slower progression to AIDS, while higher HLA-C expression was also linked with susceptibility to Crohn's disease (Apps et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Apps et al., 2013.

claim: The strongest genetic association in psoriasis is with HLA-C*06:02, thought to be mediated by HLA-C*06:02-restricted T cells.
source: In psoriasis, the strongest genetic association is with HLA-C*06:02, thought to be mediated by HLA-C*06:02-restricted T cells (Chen and Tsai, 2018; Lande et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen and Tsai, 2018 and Lande et al., 2014.

claim: Multiple HLA-C*08:02-restricted TCRs specific for the oncogenic hotspot mutation KRAS-G12D were identified in several cancer patients.
source: Most notably, multiple HLA-C*08:02-restricted TCRs specific for the oncogenic hotspot mutation KRAS-G12D were identified in several cancer patients (Tran et al., 2015; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tran et al., 2015 and 2016.

claim: Adoptive transfer of expanded KRAS-G12D-specific TILs successfully treated a patient with metastatic colorectal cancer, leading to complete regression of all but one metastatic lesion.
source: Adoptive transfer of expanded KRAS-G12D-specific TILs successfully treated a patient with metastatic colorectal cancer, leading to complete regression of all but one metastatic lesion (Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tran et al., 2016.

claim: The remaining lesion after TIL therapy lost HLA-C*08:02 from its genome, demonstrating that HLA-C-restricted T cells can mediate effective antitumor responses.
source: The remaining lesion lost HLA-C*08:02 from its genome demonstrating conclusively that HLA-C-restricted T cells can mediate effective antitumor responses (Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tran et al., 2016.

claim: HLA-C is the most recently evolved classical HLA-I gene, present in only humans and other apes.
source: HLA-C is the most recently evolved classical HLA-I gene, present in only humans and other apes, and has several unique features (Adams and Parham, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adams and Parham, 2001.

claim: HLA-C is expressed on fetal extravillous trophoblast cells, making it the most polymorphic molecule expressed at the maternal–fetal interface.
source: HLA-C, not HLA-A or HLA-B, is expressed on fetal extravillous trophoblast cells, making it the most polymorphic molecule expressed at the maternal–fetal interface (King et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King et al., 2000.

claim: All HLA-C allotypes serve as ligands for the killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR).
source: In addition, all HLA-C allotypes serve as ligands for the killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR), whereas only a subset of HLA-A and HLA-B allotypes bind KIRs (Hilton and Parham, 2017; Moesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hilton and Parham, 2017 and Moesta et al., 2008.

claim: Only a subset of HLA-A and HLA-B allotypes bind KIRs.
source: In addition, all HLA-C allotypes serve as ligands for the killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIR), whereas only a subset of HLA-A and HLA-B allotypes bind KIRs (Hilton and Parham, 2017; Moesta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hilton and Parham, 2017 and Moesta et al., 2008.

claim: C1 HLA-C allotypes carry Ser77 and Asn80 and are ligands for the inhibitory receptors KIR2DL2/3.
source: C1 HLA-C allotypes carry Ser77 and Asn80 and are ligands for the inhibitory receptors KIR2DL2/3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C1 HLA-C and is supported by the literature.

claim: The inhibitory receptor KIR2DL1 binds C2 HLA-C allotypes, which carry Asn77 and Lys80.
source: The inhibitory receptor KIR2DL1 binds C2 HLA-C allotypes, which carry Asn77 and Lys80.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C2 HLA-C and is supported by the literature.

claim: The KIR discriminate C1 and C2 HLA-C largely via position 44 in the KIR and direct interactions with HLA-C position 80.
source: The KIR discriminate C1 and C2 HLA-C largely via position 44 in the KIR (Winter and Long, 1997) and direct interactions with HLA-C position 80 (Boyington et al., 2000; Boyington and Sun, 2002; Fan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Winter and Long, 1997; Boyington et al., 2000; Boyington and Sun, 2002; Fan et al., 2001.

claim: Genetic association studies link C1/C2 status and the presence or absence of specific KIR-HLA combinations with risk of multiple human diseases.
source: Genetic association studies link C1/C2 status and the presence or absence of specific KIR-HLA combinations with risk of multiple human diseases, including cancer, infectious diseases, autoimmunity, and disorders of pregnancy (Hiby et al., 2004; Khakoo et al., 2004; Kulkarni et al., 2008; Littera et al., 2016; Parham and Moffett, 2013; Rajagopalan and Long, 2005; Venstrom et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic association studies.

claim: HLA-C*08:02 and HLA-C*05:01 differ only by the C1/C2 dimorphism defined by positions 77 and 80.
source: We compared TCR9a and TCR10 recognition of HLA-C*08:02 (C1) with that of HLA-C*05:01, a C2 allotype that is identical in sequence to HLA-C*08:02 apart from the C1/C2 defining residues at positions 77 and 80 (Sim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sim et al., 2017 and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 28 different 'self' peptides eluted from HLA-C*05:01 bound to both HLA-C*05:01 (C2) and HLA-C*08:02 (C1).
source: In a previous study, we showed that 28 different 'self' peptides eluted from HLA-C*05:01 bound to both HLA-C*05:01 (C2) and HLA-C*08:02 (C1), suggesting a minimal impact of the C1/C2 dimorphism on peptide binding to HLA-C (Sim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sim et al., 2017.

claim: TCR9a is specific for G12D-9mer (GADGVGKSA).
source: TCR9a is specific for G12D-9mer (GADGVGKSA), while TCR10 is specific for G12D-10mer (GADGVGKSAL) (Sim et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sim et al., 2020 and Tran et al., 2016.

claim: TCR10 is specific for G12D-10mer (GADGVGKSAL).
source: TCR9a is specific for G12D-9mer (GADGVGKSA), while TCR10 is specific for G12D-10mer (GADGVGKSAL) (Sim et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sim et al., 2020 and Tran et al., 2016.

claim: TCR9a and TCR10 do not share TCR V genes and recognize their peptide antigens in different ways.
source: TCR9a and TCR10 do not share TCR V genes and recognize their peptide antigens in different ways (Sim et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sim et al., 2020 and Tran et al., 2016.

claim: Both the 9mer and 10mer G12D but not their WT KRAS peptides activated their respective TCR9a and TCR10 expressing T cells in the presence of C*08.
source: As expected, both the 9mer and 10mer G12D but not their WT KRAS peptides activated their respective TCR9a and TCR10 expressing T cells in the presence of C*08 (Figure 1C and D; Sim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D and citation to Sim et al., 2020.

claim: No activation of TCR9a was observed when the 9mer G12D KRAS peptide was presented by C*05.
source: Notably, we observed no activation of TCR9a and only weak activation of TCR10 when the 9mer and 10mer G12D KRAS peptides were presented by C*05, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Only weak activation of TCR10 was observed when the 10mer G12D KRAS peptide was presented by C*05.
source: Notably, we observed no activation of TCR9a and only weak activation of TCR10 when the 9mer and 10mer G12D KRAS peptides were presented by C*05, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: G12D-9mer loaded on C*05 did not activate Jurkat-TCR9a cells in TAP-deficient cell experiments.
source: These experiments yielded similar results using a different functional readout (expression of CD69), as G12D-9mer loaded on C*05 did not activate Jurkat-TCR9a cells, while G12D-10mer loaded on C*05 did stimulate Jurkat-TCR10 cells but required higher peptide concentrations than when loaded on C*08 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: G12D-10mer loaded on C*05 stimulated Jurkat-TCR10 cells but required higher peptide concentrations than when loaded on C*08.
source: These experiments yielded similar results using a different functional readout (expression of CD69), as G12D-9mer loaded on C*05 did not activate Jurkat-TCR9a cells, while G12D-10mer loaded on C*05 did stimulate Jurkat-TCR10 cells but required higher peptide concentrations than when loaded on C*08 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: G12D-9mer only stabilized C*08 and not C*05 in peptide loading assays.
source: However, G12D-9mer only stabilized C*08 and not C*05, while G12D-10mer stabilized both allotypes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: G12D-10mer stabilized both C*08 and C*05 allotypes in peptide loading assays.
source: However, G12D-9mer only stabilized C*08 and not C*05, while G12D-10mer stabilized both allotypes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Substitution of pΩ Ala to Leu in G12D-9mer (A18L-9mer) improved binding to HLA-C*08:02.
source: We previously demonstrated that substitution of pΩ Ala to Leu in G12D-9mer (A18L-9mer: 10GADGVGKSL) improved binding to HLA-C*08:02, and T cell recognition by Jurkat-TCR9a (Sim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sim et al., 2020.

claim: A18L-9mer bound C*05 well.
source: Similarly, A18L-9mer bound C*05 well (Figure 2A and B) and stimulated Jurkat-TCR9a cells (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: A18L-9mer stimulated Jurkat-TCR9a cells.
source: Similarly, A18L-9mer bound C*05 well (Figure 2A and B) and stimulated Jurkat-TCR9a cells (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The inability of G12D-9mer to bind C*05 accounts for its lack of activation of Jurkat-TCR9a cells.
source: Thus, the inability of G12D-9mer to bind C*05 accounts for its lack of activation of Jurkat-TCR9a cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the peptide binding data (Figure 2) and T cell activation data (Figure 1).

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism selectively impacts peptide binding to HLA-C in a sequence-dependent manner.
source: Further, these data suggest that the C1/C2 dimorphism selectively impacts peptide binding to HLA-C in a sequence-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential binding of G12D-9mer and A18L-9mer to C*05 and C*08.

claim: The five most abundant pΩ residues (Leu, Val, Ile, Phe, and Met) were the same in both C*08 and C*05, accounting for 97% of C*08 and 98% of C*05 sequences.
source: We first compared the immunopeptidomes of C*08 and C*05 as the residues that form the pΩ binding pocket of C*08 and C*05 are identical and accordingly the five most abundant pΩ residues (Leu, Val, Ile, Phe, and Met) were the same in both allotypes, accounting for 97% of C*08% and 98% of C*05 sequences (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Leucine was the most common pΩ in both C*08 and C*05 but had a higher frequency in C*08 peptides (73%) than C*05 (37%).
source: Leucine was the most common pΩ in both allotypes but had a higher frequency in C*08 peptides than C*05 (C*08 = 73%, C*05 = 37%) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Among 9mer peptides, the frequency of Ala at pΩ position was 1.5% in C*08, significantly higher than 0.13% in C*05.
source: Among 9mer peptides, the frequency of Ala at pΩ position was 1.5% (30 out of 1986) in C*08, significantly higher (p=0.0016 Fisher's exact test) than that of 0.13% (1 out of 732) in C*05-bound peptides (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: pΩ Ala was the amino acid most enriched in C1 allotypes, with a frequency of 1.45% ± 1.4% in C1 allotypes compared to 0.27% ± 0.19% in C2 allotypes.
source: In concordance with the comparison of C*05 and C*08 immunopeptidomes, pΩ Ala was the one most enriched in C1 allotypes, with a frequency of 1.45% ± 1.4% in C1 allotypes compared to 0.27% ± 0.19% in C2 allotypes (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: C1 allotypes bind peptides with pΩ Ala to a greater extent than C2 allotypes.
source: Thus, C1 allotypes bind peptides with pΩ Ala to a greater extent than C2 allotypes, consistent with the ability of G12D-9mer to bind C*08 and not C*05.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on immunopeptidomics analysis (Figure 2) and peptide binding experiments.

claim: TCR9a bound to HLA-C*08 in the presence of G12D-9mer peptide with 16 nM affinity.
source: While TCR9a bound to the C1 allotype HLA-C*08 in the presence of G12D-9mer peptide with 16 nM affinity (Sim et al., 2020), it displayed a binding affinity of 108 nM for the C2 allotype HLA-C*05 in the presence of Leu anchor variant of G12D-9mer, an approximately sevenfold affinity reduction compared to the C1 allotype (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sim et al., 2020.

claim: TCR9a displayed a binding affinity of 108 nM for HLA-C*05 in the presence of A18L-9mer, an approximately sevenfold affinity reduction compared to C*08.
source: While TCR9a bound to the C1 allotype HLA-C*08 in the presence of G12D-9mer peptide with 16 nM affinity (Sim et al., 2020), it displayed a binding affinity of 108 nM for the C2 allotype HLA-C*05 in the presence of Leu anchor variant of G12D-9mer, an approximately sevenfold affinity reduction compared to the C1 allotype (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: TCR10 bound C*05:01-G12D-10mer with KD = 13 ± 6 μM by steady-state kinetics.
source: By steady-state kinetics, TCR10 binding was less than twofold weaker to C*05:01-G12D-10mer (KD = 13 ± 6 μM) than C*08:02-G12D-10mer (KD = 8 ± 5 μM) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: TCR10 bound C*08:02-G12D-10mer with KD = 8 ± 5 μM by steady-state kinetics.
source: By steady-state kinetics, TCR10 binding was less than twofold weaker to C*05:01-G12D-10mer (KD = 13 ± 6 μM) than C*08:02-G12D-10mer (KD = 8 ± 5 μM) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by SPR data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: TCR10 had almost 20-fold slower on rate with C*05:01-G12D-10mer (Kon = 6.2 ± 1.2 × 10³ M⁻¹ s⁻¹) than with C*08:02-G12D-10mer (Kon = 1.2 ± 0.9 × 10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹).
source: However, by kinetic analysis of the binding curves (Figure 3G), TCR10 had almost 20-fold slower on rate with C*05:01-G12D-10mer (Kon = 6.2 ± 1.2 × 103 M–1 s–1) than with C*08:02-G12D-10mer (Kon = 1.2 ± 0.9 × 105 M–1 s–1).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis of SPR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Neither TCR9a nor TCR10 make direct contacts to HLA-C positions Ser 77 and Asn 80.
source: Neither TCR9a nor TCR10 make direct contacts to HLA-C positions Ser 77 and Asn 80 (Sim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sim et al., 2020 and structural data in Figure 4.

claim: The crystal structure of TCR9a in complex with C*05-A18L-9mer was determined to a high resolution of 1.9 Å.
source: To understand the impact of C2 residues Asn 77 and Lys 80 on T cell recognition, we determined the crystal structure of TCR9a in complex with C*05-A18L-9mer to a high resolution of 1.9 Å (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure determination described in the methods and results.

claim: TCR9a adopted the same binding mode when in complex with C*05 as in the C*08 complex structure.
source: TCR9a adopted the same binding mode when in complex with C*05, as in the C*08 complex structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All contacts observed between TCR9a and the C2 HLA-C*05 are conserved in the structure of TCR9a complexed with C*08.
source: All these contacts observed between TCR9a and the C2 HLA-C*05 are conserved in the structure of TCR9a complexed with C*08 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4B-D.

claim: The dimorphic residues 77 and 80 on the C2 HLA-C*05 do not interact with TCR9a.
source: Like the C1 HLA-C*08, the dimorphic residues 77 and 80 on the C2 HLA-C*05 also do not interact with TCR9a.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The closest TCR residue to HLA-C position 77 or 80 is Glu 49 of the TCRβ chain, which is greater than 7 Å away from HLA-C position 80.
source: The closest TCR residue to HLA-C position 77 or 80 is Glu 49 of the TCRβ chain that interacts with Lys p7 of the peptide but is greater than 7 Å away from HLA-C position 80.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the TCR9a-C*05 complex.

claim: Position 77 side chain is orientated directly into the peptide-binding groove, while position 80 sits atop the α1-helix.
source: The position 77 side chain is orientated directly into the PBG, while position 80 sits atop the α1-helix (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural visualization shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Position 77 is Ser in C*08 (C1) and Asn in C*05 (C2) and both form an h-bond of the same distance with the amide of the terminal peptide bond between pΩ and p8 (pΩ-1).
source: Position 77 is Ser in C*08 (C1) and Asn in C*05 (C2) and both form an h-bond of the same distance with the amide of the terminal peptide bond between pΩ and p8 (pΩ-1) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Peptide p8 was higher out of the peptide-binding groove in C*05 compared to C*08.
source: Comparing the structures of C*05 and C*08, the HLA-C α1-helices were displaced relative to each other and peptide p8 was higher out of the PBG in C*05 compared to C*08 (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The distance between the Cα of peptide p8 and the Cβ of HLA-C position 77 was 4.7 Å in C*08 and 5.7 Å in C*05.
source: This distance was 4.7 Å and 5.7 Å in the C*08 and C*05 structures, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The difference between the Cα of peptide p8 and HLA-C 77 Cβ was maintained between C1 and C2 HLA-C structures (C1 = 4.6 ± 0.11 Å, C2 = 5.7 ± 0.22 Å).
source: We observed that the difference between the Cα of peptide p8 and HLA-C 77 Cβ was maintained between C1 and C2 HLA-C structures (C1 = 4.6 ± 0.11 Å, C2 = 5.7 ± 0.22 Å) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of 12 HLA-C structures shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In all five C1 allotype structures, the p8 side chain was within van der Waals range of Val 76 (3.3–4.0 Å).
source: In all five C1 allotype structures, the p8 side chain was within van der Waals range of Val 76 (3.3–4.0 Å).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of multiple HLA-C structures shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The p8 side chain was out of contact range with Val 76 in all but one C2 HLA-C structures.
source: In contrast, the p8 side chain was out of contact range with Val 76 in all but one C2 HLA-C structures (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: The torsion angle of the terminal peptide bond orientates p8 towards the α1 helix in C1 allotypes and out of the groove in C2 allotypes.
source: This appears to be due in part to the torsion angle of the terminal peptide bond that orientates p8 towards the α1 helix in C1 allotypes and out of the groove in C2 allotypes (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism impacts the position and orientation of the peptide at pΩ-1.
source: Thus, the C1/C2 dimorphism impacts the position and orientation of the peptide at pΩ-1, suggesting that position 77 is the major determinant of the difference between C*05 and C*08.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Position 77 is the major determinant of the difference between C*05 and C*08.
source: Thus, the C1/C2 dimorphism impacts the position and orientation of the peptide at pΩ-1, suggesting that position 77 is the major determinant of the difference between C*05 and C*08.
evidence: This is suggested by structural analysis and supported by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 5K.

claim: C*05-N77S recovered Jurkat-TCR9a responses, though not completely.
source: The lack of stimulation of Jurkat-TCR9a by C*05 was minimally impacted by C*05-K80N, while C*05-N77S recovered Jurkat-TCR9a responses, though not completely (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Stimulation of Jurkat-TCR10 cells by HLA-C*05:01 was not improved by single substitutions at positions 77 and 80.
source: In contrast, stimulation of Jurkat-TCR10 cells by HLA-C*05:01 was not improved by single substitutions at positions 77 and 80, suggesting a synergistic effect of positions 77 and 80 on recognition of HLA-C*08:02 by TCR10.
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: There was a weak correlation (r = 0.46) at p7 and no correlation in amino acid usage (r = –0.01) at p8 (pΩ-1) between C*08 and C*05 immunopeptidomes.
source: In contrast, there was a weak correlation (r = 0.46) at p7 and no correlation in amino acid usage (r = –0.01) at p8 (pΩ-1) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At pΩ-1, Ala and Ser made up over 30% of sequences unique to C*08, but only 5% of sequences unique to C*05.
source: At pΩ-1, Ala and Ser made up over 30% of sequences unique to C*08, but only 5% of sequences unique to C*05.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Leu, Lys, and Arg were found in approximately 40% of sequences unique to C*05, but only 7% of sequences unique to C*08.
source: In contrast, Leu, Lys, and Arg were found in approximately 40% of sequences unique to C*05, but only 7% of sequences unique to C*08 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At p8, C1 allotypes are enriched for Ser, Ala, and Pro, while C2 allotypes are enriched for Phe, Leu, Lys, Met, Arg, Trp, and Tyr.
source: We found that at p8, C1 allotypes are enriched for Ser, Ala, and Pro, while C2 allotypes are enriched for Phe, Leu, Lys, Met, Arg, Trp, and Tyr (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics analysis shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a strong correlation between amino acid enrichment at p8 in C2 allotypes and amino acid side-chain volume.
source: There was a strong correlation between amino acid enrichment at p8 in C2 allotypes and amino acid side-chain volume, demonstrating that the C1/C2 dimorphism imposes a size constraint on the peptides bound to HLA-C (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism imposes a size constraint on the peptides bound to HLA-C.
source: There was a strong correlation between amino acid enrichment at p8 in C2 allotypes and amino acid side-chain volume, demonstrating that the C1/C2 dimorphism imposes a size constraint on the peptides bound to HLA-C (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: In peptides eluted from C1 allotypes, the preference for smaller residues at p8 was accentuated in peptides with pΩ-Ala compared to those with pΩ-Leu.
source: In peptides eluted from C1 allotypes, the preference for smaller residues at p8 was accentuated in peptides with pΩ-Ala compared to those with pΩ-Leu (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that size at pΩ-1 is especially important for peptides with pΩ-Ala.
evidence: This is supported by immunopeptidomics analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Substitution at p8 in G12D-9mer to Leu, Lys, and Arg substantially increased the EC50 by approximately 1000-fold.
source: Stimulation of Jurkat-TCR9a by C*08 cells loaded with G12D-9mer p8 substitutions to Leu, Lys, and Arg substantially increased the EC50 by approximately 1000-fold, while substitution to Ala, Gly, Glu, Val had a minimal impact on the EC50 (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Substitution at p8 in G12D-9mer to Ala, Gly, Glu, Val had a minimal impact on the EC50.
source: Stimulation of Jurkat-TCR9a by C*08 cells loaded with G12D-9mer p8 substitutions to Leu, Lys, and Arg substantially increased the EC50 by approximately 1000-fold, while substitution to Ala, Gly, Glu, Val had a minimal impact on the EC50 (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: p8 substitutions in A18L-9mer to Lys, Arg, and Leu increased the EC50 by roughly 10-fold.
source: The same p8 substitutions in A18L-9mer had much less impact on Jurkat-TCR9a stimulation; however, p8 Lys, Arg, and Leu increased the EC50 by roughly 10-fold (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is supported by functional data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The G12D-9mer and G12D-10mer are considered public or shared neoantigens due to the high frequency of cancers with KRAS-G12D mutations.
source: The G12D-9mer and G12D-10mer are considered public or shared neoantigens due to the high frequency of cancers with KRAS-G12D mutations (Cox et al., 2014; Pearlman et al., 2021; Stephen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cox et al., 2014; Pearlman et al., 2021; Stephen et al., 2014.

claim: The ability of C*05 to bind G12D-10mer means HLA-C*05:01-positive individuals may be eligible for immunotherapies targeting KRAS-G12D.
source: The ability of C*05 to bind G12D-10mer means HLA-C*05:01-positive individuals may be eligible for such therapies; however, identifying a more sensitive receptor than TCR10 would be needed to translate these findings for clinical application.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings that C*05 can bind G12D-10mer.

claim: T cells, like NK cells, can discriminate between the dimorphic HLA-C allotypes.
source: Finally, our study establishes that T cells, like NK cells, can discriminate between the dimorphic HLA-C allotypes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: The C1/C2 dimorphism defines two distinct peptide-binding groove structures that impose size constraints at pΩ-1.
source: Specifically, the C1/C2 dimorphism defines two distinct PBG structures that impose size constraints at pΩ-1 and allow C1 but not C2 allotypes to bind peptides with shorter pΩ anchors, like Ala in G12D-9mer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis (Figure 5) and immunopeptidomics data (Figure 6).

claim: C1 but not C2 allotypes can bind peptides with shorter pΩ anchors, like Ala in G12D-9mer.
source: Specifically, the C1/C2 dimorphism defines two distinct PBG structures that impose size constraints at pΩ-1 and allow C1 but not C2 allotypes to bind peptides with shorter pΩ anchors, like Ala in G12D-9mer.
evidence: This is supported by peptide binding data in Figure 2 showing G12D-9mer binds C*08 but not C*05.

claim: As Asn (C2) is larger than Ser (C1), it results in peptide pΩ-1 protruding out of the groove, thus permitting larger amino acids at pΩ-1 in C2 allotypes compared to C1.
source: As Asn (C2) is larger than Ser (C1), it results in peptide pΩ-1 protruding out of the groove, thus permitting larger amino acids at pΩ-1 in C2 allotypes compared to C1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis in Figure 5.

claim: In C1, pΩ-1 sits lower in the groove, restricting pΩ-1 side chains to smaller residues to avoid clashing with HLA-C position Val 76.
source: In C1, pΩ-1 sits lower in the groove, restricting pΩ-1 side chains to smaller residues to avoid clashing with HLA-C position Val 76.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis in Figure 5.

claim: A canonical pΩ anchor can accommodate unfavorable p8 residues, likely via orientating p8 side chain out of the groove like peptides in C2 allotypes.
source: Further, the penalty imposed for large residues at p8 was diminished with A18L-9mer, suggesting a canonical pΩ anchor can accommodate unfavorable p8 residues, likely via orientating p8 side chain out of the groove like peptides in C2 allotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional data in Figure 7 comparing G12D-9mer and A18L-9mer.

claim: In C1 allotypes, the additional contacts between Val 76 and p8 may explain the ability of C*08:02 to bind peptides with short, suboptimal pΩ anchors.
source: In C1 allotypes, the additional contacts between Val 76 and p8 may explain the ability of C*08:02 to bind peptides with short, suboptimal pΩ anchors.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis in Figure 5.

claim: pΩ-1 in C2, which is higher in the peptide-binding groove and orientated away from the α1 helix, is unable to contact Val 76 and therefore cannot support peptides with pΩ Ala.
source: In contrast, pΩ-1 in C2, which is higher in the PBG and orientated away from the α1 helix, is unable to contact Val 76 and therefore cannot support peptides with pΩ Ala.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis in Figure 5 and peptide binding data in Figure 2.

claim: The most likely explanation for diminished TCR binding in the presence of C2 residues is conformational flexibility.
source: The most likely explanation for diminished TCR binding in the presence of C2 residues is that of conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that TCR contacts are conserved but binding is weaker.

claim: The ability to make the same contacts with C*08 in C*05 likely requires more energetically unfavorable conformational changes, in either peptide, HLA-C, or both.
source: Clearly, TCR9a and TCR10 can bind C*05; however, the ability to make the same contacts with C*08 in C*05 likely requires more energetically unfavorable conformational changes, in either peptide, HLA-C, or both, exemplified by the slow on rate of TCR10 with C*05-G12D-10mer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the slow on rate observed for TCR10 with C*05 in Figure 3G.

claim: Viral escape mutants may eliminate T cell recognition of C1 allotypes by increasing side chain size at pΩ-1.
source: For example, in infectious diseases, viral escape mutants may eliminate T cell recognition of C1 allotypes by increasing side chain size at pΩ-1.
evidence: This is speculation about potential implications of the findings.

claim: Escape mutants that substitute pΩ to smaller residues like Ala may escape T cell recognition of C2 HLA-C but not C1.
source: Similarly, escape mutants that substitute pΩ to smaller residues like Ala may escape T cell recognition of C2 HLA-C but not C1.
evidence: This is speculation about potential implications of the findings.

claim: For peptide vaccines, pΩ-1 size could be optimized depending on whether the peptide targets a C1 or C2 HLA-C allotype.
source: For peptide vaccines, pΩ-1 size could be optimized depending on whether the peptide targets a C1 or C2 HLA-C allotype.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: HIV-infected individuals can respond to the same epitope (SAEPVPLQL) if they carry HLA-Cw5 or HLA-Cw8.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that HIV-infected individuals can respond to the same epitope (SAEPVPLQL) if they carry HLA-Cw5 or HLA-Cw8 (Addo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Addo et al., 2001.

claim: The differences in amino acid preferences at pΩ-1 may have consequences for KIR recognition of HLA-C as this residue is central to the KIR binding site.
source: In particular, the differences in amino acid preferences at pΩ-1 may have enormous consequences for KIR recognition of HLA-C as this residue is central to the KIR binding site (Boyington et al., 2000; Boyington and Sun, 2002; Fan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and supported by citations about KIR binding sites.
